title: Your place in the story
hook: the story isn't over; you are part of what comes next

segments.voice: Yesterday, your family's story, and your line was ask your elders. Did you ask your question, and listen to the end? Today, the last page of this part of the long story, and the blank one after it. Day one thousand forty-six.

A notebook, written almost to the end. The last few lines are crowded: a kitchen on a highway, a turban explained at a table on a lawn, a river cleaned by hand, a forest on a scrap of dirt, a grandfather's story in a parked car. Then a page with nothing on it. Not torn out. Just waiting. That's where this part of the path has brought us, through the twentieth century and into today. The pen is on the table. Whose hand picks it up? Today, your place in the story.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK, NEARLY FULL.` → `THE CROWDED LAST LINES.` → `A BLANK PAGE, WAITING.`

segments.voice: First, the story isn't over. These last weeks weren't about the past. They were about Sikhs right now: in parliaments and at protests, in kitchens and classrooms, cleaning rivers, planting trees, arguing honestly about caste and about who may sing kirtan. Sikhs hold that the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru and the Khalsa Panth carries the work on. That means the story keeps being written by ordinary people. Second, what an ordinary day looks like. At Ang 305, Guru Ram Das describes the one who calls himself a Sikh of the True Guru: rising early, bathing, remembering the Name, and keeping it through the day, sitting or standing, with every breath and every bite. Nothing in that list is grand. It's a day, done with attention. Third, the surprise at the end. The same hymn closes with Guru Ram Das, a Guru, asking for the dust of the feet of that kind of Sikh: the one who remembers the Name and helps others remember it too. The Guru bows to the ordinary day. Fourth, your place. Whether you're Sikh, learning about Sikhs, or here for someone you love, the story you've heard this year goes on through small acts. A plate washed. A question asked. A neighbor's turban understood. A promise kept. Tomorrow, the path turns to the calendar of memory, the days Sikhs gather to remember. Today, the line is simple: the story goes on.
screen: `SIKHS RIGHT NOW, NOT ONLY THEN.` · `ANG 305: AN ORDINARY DAY.` · `THE GURU ASKS FOR THE DUST.` · `SMALL ACTS CARRY IT ON.` · then, large: `THE STORY GOES ON.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the blank page. Sit, and let your breath slow. Picture that notebook, open to the empty page. Breathe in, and ask: what's one thing I could do today that would be worth telling someone, years from now? Not a big thing. Something true. Breathe out, and let one answer arrive. Don't judge it. Just see it on the page, in your own handwriting. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Your place in the story. The long story of the Sikhs isn't finished, and it keeps being written through ordinary days lived with attention, the kind of day Guru Ram Das honors. Today's word.
screen: `YOUR PLACE IN THE STORY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the story goes on. Today, do the one thing you saw on the blank page, the thing worth telling. Tomorrow, the calendar of memory begins. Day one thousand forty-six.
